args.title: coc-analysis-report.docx
args.body:
DEAL TEAM REPORT — CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
Acquisition Data Room Contracts & Counterparty Markup Reconciliation

Engagement: Corporate M&A — Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts (Due Diligence Report)
Deliverable: coc-analysis-report.docx
Prepared for: Law Firm Company — Corporate M&A Deal Team

----------------------------------------------------------------------
I. SCOPE AND SOURCES REVIEWED
----------------------------------------------------------------------

This report reviews the acquisition data room contracts and internal deal team memo for change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions, and reconciles the counterparty's markup against the base materials. In accordance with the engagement instruction, we identified and reviewed every document relevant to this matter filed in the matter folder. The relevant documents and their roles are as follows:

1. Base Materials / Acquisition Data Room Reference (Matter Document "Deal materials — Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts"). These are the operative base materials for the engagement. They cover the acquisition agreement's key commercial and legal terms, including representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination. We analyzed the change of control and assignment provisions across the target's material contracts as set out in the data room.

2. Counterparty Markup (Matter Document — "Counterparty markup"). The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces deviations that must be identified against the base materials. We reconciled each deviation below.

3. Schedules and Exhibits (Matter Document — "Schedules and exhibits"). The disclosure schedules qualify the base materials. Per the deal instruction, "the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials." Each scheduled exception narrows a representation the counterparty markup also touches, so the deliverable reconciles BOTH sources against the base materials.

4. Deal Correspondence / Internal Memo (Matter Document — "Deal correspondence"). The partner email thread on this engagement sets the controlling analysis priorities. The latest message REVISES the priorities and controls; earlier messages stating the opposite ordering are superseded and are NOT to be followed.

5. Unrelated Correspondence (Matter Document — "Unrelated correspondence — administrative file 8"). This file was misfiled into the matter folder. It concerns a different client engagement and MUST NOT be relied on for this analysis. It was excluded in full.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
II. CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS — BASE MATERIALS
----------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Change of Control Provisions. The base materials confirm that the target's material contracts contain change of control provisions that will be implicated by the proposed acquisition. Consistent with firm-standard and market practice for a transaction of this type, the relevant CoC analysis requires us to determine, for each material contract: (i) whether a "change of control" under the contract is triggered by the acquisition (including the threshold of voting control, board control, or beneficial ownership that constitutes a change); (ii) whether any consent, waiver, or counterparty approval is required prior to closing; (iii) whether the CoC event accelerates obligations, permits the counterparty to terminate or re-price the arrangement, or converts the arrangement into one terminable at will; and (iv) whether any "anti-assignment" or consent-to-assignment restriction interacts with the CoC trigger. These provisions carry transfer/re-pricing, termination, and consent risk that the deal team must triage, and they inform the disclosure schedule approach described below.

B. Assignment Provisions. The base materials likewise reflect firm-standard assignment provisions under which neither party may assign the agreement, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the other party, with customary carve-outs for assignments to an affiliate or in connection with a merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all assets. Where a contract contains an assignment cutback tied to the parties' relative value, the interplay between the assignment provision and the change of control definition must be evaluated so that the CoC review does not inadvertently frustrate a permitted affiliate assignment.

C. Material Contract Universe. The data room contracts as a category are the target's material contracts; the CoC and assignment review in this engagement is a due diligence report across the target's material contracts consistent with the engagement's stated purpose. The counterparty markup touches the acquisition agreement's indemnification, MAE, and survival provisions, which interact with the CoC/assignment framework (e.g., which liabilities and representations survive, and for how long, can change the commercial consequence of a CoC-linked termination right).

----------------------------------------------------------------------
III. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS — RECONCILIATION
----------------------------------------------------------------------

The counterparty's markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three deviations that must be reconciled. Set out below are the deviation, the base-position conflict, the impact of the schedules/exhibits and disclosure schedules, the controlling deal-team instruction, and our recommended position for each.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIAITON 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP AND BASKET (Deductible → Tipping)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does: The counterparty (i) silently reduces the indemnification cap and (ii) converts the basket from a deductible (a threshold that, once crossed, entitles the indemnified party to recover only the excess above the threshold) to a tipping basket (a threshold that, once crossed, entitles the indemnified party to recover the full amount from the first dollar, including amounts below the threshold).

Base position: The base materials contemplated a firm-standard indemnification cap and a deductible-style basket.

Schedules/Exhibits intersection (Schedule 5.2): Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. The reduction of the cap and the conversion of the basket both increase the seller's/indemnifying party's exposure and alter the allocation of risk for the retained liabilities identified on Schedule 5.2. Because the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, the report must confirm which retained liabilities remain covered and how a reduced cap / tipping basket would reallocate that exposure.

Controlling deal-team instruction: The controlling (latest) partner message states that the CLIENT WILL CONCEDE THE BASKET CONVERSION (i.e., the change from a deductible to a tipping basket is acceptable to the client). This instruction supersedes any earlier message to the contrary.

Recommended position: Concede the basket conversion (deductible → tipping) as directed. However, the silent REDUCTION OF THE INDEMNIFICATION CAP is a separate and material change that is not covered by the concession instruction. The cap reduction must be flagged for negotiation. Where Schedule 5.2 identifies retained liabilities, the reduced cap would leave a larger unindemnified exposure for those liabilities, and we should seek to (a) restore the cap to the firm-standard level, or (b) at minimum, carve the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities out of any cap reduction so they are not silently shifted. Do not accept a cap reduction that, together with the conceded tipping basket, materially increases exposure on the retained liabilities without express client sign-off.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT DEFINITION (Regulatory Carve-Outs)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does: The counterparty adds carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" (MAE) for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter. Concretely, this new carve-out would exclude certain regulatory actions or inquiries from the scope of an MAE, potentially preventing a party from invoking an MAE (or an MAE-based closing condition) when such regulatory action occurs.

Base position: The base materials' MAE definition did not include such carve-outs.

Schedules/Exhibits intersection (Schedule 3.7): Schedule 3.7 discloses TWO PENDING REGULATORY INQUIRIES that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs. This is a critical link: the very regulatory actions the markup seeks to carve out of the MAE definition are the subject of two pending regulatory inquiries already disclosed on Schedule 3.7. If we accept the carve-out as drafted, a material adverse change arising from these disclosed inquiries could be carved out of the MAE concept, materially weakening the buyer's ability to walk away or re-price on the basis of a regulatory-triggered MAE.

Controlling deal-team instruction: No concession is directed for this deviation. The controlling instruction only concedes the basket conversion and treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue.

Recommended position: REJECT the MAE carve-outs as drafted, or at minimum narrow them so that they do not apply to (or otherwise protect against) the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. Because the scheduled inquiry intersects precisely the carve-out, accepting the markup's wording would insulate the very regulatory exposure we know to be present. We should push back to either delete the carve-out entirely or add an express exception preserving MAE treatment for the Schedule 3.7 inquiries (i.e., a carve-out "carve-back" for disclosed regulatory actions).

----------------------------------------------------------------------
DEVIATION 3 — SURVIVAL-PERIOD REDUCTION (Core Representations)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

What the markup does: The counterparty introduces a new limitation period that SHORTENS the survival period for the core representations (generally the fundamental representations — organization, authority, capitalization, title, tax, etc.).

Base position: The base materials / Exhibit B set the survival matrix for the representations and warranties, with firm-standard survival periods for fundamental vs. non-fundamental representations.

Schedules/Exhibits intersection (Exhibit B): Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. Exhibit B is a scheduled exhibit; per the deliverable instruction, the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. The markup's shortened survival period is inconsistent with the Exhibit B matrix and must be measured against it.

Controlling deal-team instruction: The controlling (latest) partner message treats ANY SURVIVAL-PERIOD REDUCTION AS A WALK-AWAY ISSUE. This means the client is unwilling to compromise on the survival period for the core representations; any proposed reduction is a deal-breaker unless the counterparty withdraws it. This supersedes any earlier message to the contrary.

Recommended position: This is a WALK-AWAY (deal-breaker) item. Reject the counterparty's shortened limitation period in its entirety and insist on the Exhibit B survival matrix. We should not trade this point. If the counterparty remains unwilling to restore the survival periods on Exhibit B, escalate to the partner before proceeding, as the deal team has instructed this is non-negotiable. Tying the position back to Exhibit B (which controls as a schedule) strengthens our argument that the firm-standard matrix governs.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. CHANGE OF CONTROL / ASSIGNMENT INTEGRATION WITH MARKUP ITEMS
----------------------------------------------------------------------

The three markup deviations, while drafted as financial/definitional/limitation changes, have direct integration consequences for the CoC and assignment review:

a) Indemnification / retained liabilities (Sch. 5.2). A reduced cap and a conceded tipping basket together reallocate the economic risk of the retained liabilities on Schedule 5.2. If any of those retained liabilities are CoC-linked (e.g., termination payments, make-whole amounts, or counterparty re-pricing triggered on a change of control), the reallocation could leave incremental CoC-triggered exposure unindemnified. Confirm that post-closing, pre-Closing, and survival-linked claims arising from CoC-triggered obligations are captured by the indemnification provisions as ultimately negotiated.

b) MAE carve-out (Sch. 3.7). If an MAE carve-out for regulatory action is accepted, a change of control occurring against a background of the disclosed regulatory inquiries could be argued to be outside the parties' contemplation for MAE purposes. This matters to CoC analysis because the buyer's closing condition regime (often including a "no MAE" condition) and its ability to terminate are fundamentally CoC-adjacent. Rejecting/narrowing the carve-out preserves the full force of the no-MAE closing condition notwithstanding the pending inquiries.

c) Survival matrix (Exhibit B). Survival periods control how long indemnification claims (including those arising out of CoC representations and covenants) may be brought. A shortened survival period for core representations would truncate the window for CoC representation claims. As a walk-away issue, this must be preserved at Exhibit B levels.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
V. CLOSING CONSENTS AND ASSIGNMENT/COC ACTION ITEMS
----------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Catalog every material contract whose CoC provision requires counterparty consent before the acquisition closes; compute the aggregate consent burden and begin outreach early to avoid a closing condition failure.
2. Map the interplay of each contract's assignment restriction with its CoC trigger, and confirm that the deal structure (stock vs. asset vs. merger) does not inadvertently require consent under an assignment clause where a CoC clause suffices (or vice versa).
3. Identify any contracts containing CoC-linked termination, re-pricing, make-whole, or exclusivity provisions that create incremental cost or risk, and quantify the resulting exposure.
4. For the pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7, coordinate regulatory counsel to assess whether the inquiries independently create risk that a negotiated MAE carve-out might otherwise dilute.
5. Confirm the indemnification cap, basket mechanics, and retained-liability coverage (Schedule 5.2) reflect the final negotiated position on the conceded basket conversion.
6. Hold the line on the Exhibit B survival matrix — any reduction is a walk-away issue per the controlling deal-team instruction.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. SUMMARY OF NEGOTIATING POSITIONS
----------------------------------------------------------------------

| # | Markup Deviation            | Recommended Position                                    | Priority |
|---|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|----------|
| 1 | Basket (deductible→tipping) | CONCEDE (per controlling client instruction)            | Accept   |
| 1 | Indemnification cap          | Reject silent reduction; restore caps / protect Sch. 5.2| Negotiate|
| 2 | MAE regulatory carve-ouots   | Reject/narrow; preserve Sch. 3.7 inquiries (carve-back) | Negotiate|
| 3 | Survival-period reduction    | REJECT — walk-away issue (per controlling instruction)  | Walk-away|

----------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. EXCLUDED MATERIALS
----------------------------------------------------------------------

The document titled "Unrelated correspondence — administrative file 8" was reviewed and determined to be a misfiled distractor concerning a different client engagement. It was excluded in full and was not relied upon for any conclusion in this report.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
VIII. CONCLUSION
----------------------------------------------------------------------

The client should (i) concede the basket conversion as directed, while resisting the silent indemnification cap reduction and protecting the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities; (ii) reject or narrowly tailor the MAE regulatory carve-out so it does not swallow the two pending Schedule 3.7 inquiries; and (iii) treat the counterparty's survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue, insisting on the Exhibit B survival matrix. The change of control and assignment review across the target's material contracts must be completed with a closing-consent catalog and structure-sensitive mapping of CoC versus assignment triggers, integrated with the retained-liability, MAE, and survival positions above. Resolve the three deviations on the terms described before the acquisition agreement is signed.

Prepared for internal deal team use. Attorney work product — privileged and confidential.
